steps.focus: h1 How this is kept safe
steps.aria:
- main:
  - heading "How this is kept safe" [level=1]
  - paragraph: What Foundry does, where, what it keeps, and the one limit you should know about.
  - region "What runs where":
    - heading "What runs where" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "Everything runs on this computer. The page listens on this computer only, and nothing listens on your network. Your automations and records are in this folder, private to your user:"
    - text: /tmp/journey-p4-it-TJPtMF
  - region "What leaves this computer":
    - heading "What leaves this computer" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "Foundry itself sends one thing: when you press Check and save on an AI key, one request to that provider with the key, and only if Allowed AI includes that provider. Nothing else: e-mails are drafts you send, chat messages are drafts you paste. If you use Foundry through a coding agent, what Foundry tells the agent (counts, step names, test results on pretend data) goes to that agent's AI provider under your agreement with them; the recipients and text of a real list are shown only in this page. AI builders: Mercury (Inception) only if Allowed AI says so and a key is saved; Claude Haiku (Anthropic) only if Foundry is started with it and Allowed AI says so. Neither is on by default."
  - region "What Foundry keeps, and how to delete it":
    - heading "What Foundry keeps, and how to delete it" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "Only the columns a card needs from the lists you give, the drafts it made, run records and your decisions, all in your Foundry folder, which Foundry makes private to your user each time it starts (Settings says so if it can't, for example when the folder is your home folder). Replaced lists are kept until you delete them (Settings: Delete my lists). Outside that folder: an AI key in your keychain, if you saved one; this tab's key in the browser tab; and any file you download. Foundry doesn't encrypt anything itself: if your computer's disk is encrypted, that protects these files while it is off; if it isn't, nothing does. To remove everything, delete the Foundry folder."
  - region "Keys":
    - heading "Keys" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "AI keys go into your computer's keychain. Foundry never writes them to a file, a log or the AI's view. If your computer has no keychain Foundry can use, it doesn't save the key. A keychain keeps the key from other users of this computer, not from programs running as you: on a Mac, Foundry saves it in a way that lets any program running as you read it back through the security command without asking you (from Apple's documentation; not tried on a Mac), and on Linux any program running as you can read it while your keyring is unlocked. Bringing your own AI key is free, and the key goes into your computer's keychain, never into files or logs. Preview (A keychain keeps the key from other users of this computer, not from programs running as you. On a Mac, Foundry saves the key without naming which programs may read it, so any program running as you can read it back through the security command without a prompt (from Apple's documentation of that command; not tried on a Mac). On Linux, any program running as you can read it while the keyring is unlocked.)"
      - 'link "Source: Your key, your keychain"':
        - /url: "#/claims?claim=C10"
        - text: (source)
  - region "Who can approve":
    - heading "Who can approve" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "You decide: with a click on this page, a typed yes in your own terminal, or, when Foundry finds nothing that could answer it for you, the dialog Claude Code shows you. Foundry gives your agent no tool that approves. In our tests, 10 of 10 attempts to get around your yes were refused. Not re-tested (Tested on the earlier prototype's tools and page, before the exact-list approval and the one-time links were added; that set of attempts has not been re-run against them. The ways around your yes found in the security review of 2026-10-21 (a printed link read by an agent, a hook answering the dialog, a list changed after you saw it) have their own tests now. Not covered: an agent using your terminal, or a hook Foundry can't see.)"
      - 'link "Source: Ways around your yes are refused"':
        - /url: "#/claims?claim=C02"
        - text: (source)
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Why Foundry asks once, about the whole list, rather than about each e-mail: People approve almost every single prompt (97% in one vendor's data) but reject whole plans far more often (39% versus 3%). Literature (Vendor-published numbers, not a controlled study of Foundry.)"
      - 'link "Source: Why Foundry asks once, about the whole plan"':
        - /url: "#/claims?claim=C11"
        - text: (source)
  - region "The honest limit":
    - heading "The honest limit" [level=2]
    - paragraph: A coding agent that can run commands as you on this computer could do what you can do, including approve. Foundry's link key and checks keep out other web pages and other users, not that agent.
    - paragraph: "What could close this gap: Foundry running as a separate user, approvals on a second device, or the hosted Team plan. These are options we have written down; none of them is built or scheduled."
  - region "Dialogs a hook can answer":
    - heading "Dialogs a hook can answer" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "A hook in Claude Code's settings, or in a plugin, skill or subagent, can answer Foundry's dialog without showing it to you, or change your answer. So Foundry uses that dialog only when it can look for such hooks and finds none. The line from the Connect page includes --consent, which lets Foundry read Claude Code's settings, plugins, skills and subagents on this computer, only to look for those hooks, and it looks again each time it asks. It asks you in this page instead if it finds one, if your organisation manages Claude Code, if Claude Code was started in a way that can bring hooks Foundry can't see, or if your agent isn't Claude Code.
